abstract: Munc13-4 operates as an intracellular Ca2+ sensor for regulated secretion in both immune and cancer cells. Its capacity to physically engage multiple Rab GTPases and SNARE proteins places it at the center of membrane reorganization upon intracellular Ca2+ elevation. Here, we define the mode of action of Munc13-4 during Ca2+ evoked exosome secretion in RBL-2H3 mast cells. We show that Munc13-4 coupling to Rab27a is essential to retain Munc13-4 on secretory membranes for exosome release in mast cells, contrasting with cancer cells where the Munc13-4 Rab11 axis predominates. Using simultaneous epifluorescence and total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy validated by high pressure freezing electron microscopy, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), and staged acute inhibition with Bexin 1, we demonstrate that Munc13-4 acts at the terminal post-docking stage of multivesicular body (MVB) exocytosis: acute Munc13-4 inhibition after vacuole formation leaves PM contact intact but abolishes fusion pore opening and destabilizes nascent pores. Moreover, depleting Rab27a while elevating Rab11 redirects Munc13-4 onto Rab11+ compartments in mast cells, recapitulating the cancer-cell phenotype. Together, our findings support a rapid-exchange, abundance weighted Rab partitioning model that tempers cellular Ca2+ responsiveness and governs cell type specific exosome fusion pathways, providing a mechanistic rationale for context selective modulation of pathological exosome release.
